title: Desert water discipline: cgroup quotas in liters per GB-hour
idea: From desert nomads who budget every liter: the kernel gains a water.max cgroup controller that converts each container's resident GB-hours into liters (amortized fab UPW per bit plus site WUE times memory power); over-budget pages are compressed or tiered to flash automatically, and budgets ratchet down 10x on a published schedule.
why: Makes water the binding resource, forcing compression and tiering that drive resident DRAM, and thus embedded fab and cooling water, down an order of magnitude per workload.

title: Core-memory read-modify-write: accumulate inside the restore cycle
idea: Core memories rewrote every word they read, and machines like the PDP-1 used that rewrite to increment memory in place. Do the same on destructive-read arrays: a sense amplifier with an adder/XOR in its writeback path folds an incoming gradient or count into the data during restore, demonstrated on a university-fab 1T1C or gain-cell test array.
why: Gradient accumulation and embedding/histogram updates dominate training memory traffic; accumulating during restore removes double-buffered accumulators and halves read-plus-write traffic.

title: Git-style Merkle heap: forked agent sessions share unchanged memory
idea: Represent a process's heap and KV state as a content-addressed Merkle tree of 4 KB chunks with hardware-assisted hashing; forking an agent (tree search, best-of-N, multi-agent branches) copies only the root and the diverging chunks, like git branches.
why: Agentic workloads fork state constantly; N branches cost ~1x plus deltas instead of Nx, a 5-20x DRAM saving for tree-search inference.

title: Telegraph codebook KV: position-free phrase blocks shared rack-wide
idea: Like 1880s commercial telegraph codes that replaced common phrases with five-letter codewords, frequently reused segments (system prompts, tool schemas, popular documents) get codewords whose KV is computed once in a position-independent form and kept in rack-pooled memory. Sessions store only codeword references, and RoPE re-rotation plus a small boundary-correction pass place the phrase at any offset at read time.
why: Unlike prefix caching, reuse works anywhere in the context; for agent/RAG workloads where 50-90% of tokens are repeated chunks, per-session KV drops 2-10x.

title: Memory whose precision fades with page age
idea: Software tags pages as tolerant (caches, embeddings, KV, media buffers). A memory-controller engine re-quantizes each tolerant page as it ages through epochs of seconds, then minutes, then hours: 16, 8, 4 and finally 2 bits per value, with per-block scales. It releases the frames this frees. Re-access re-promotes the page but cannot restore lost bits, much like the fading of human memory.
why: Tolerant data is 30-60% of the footprint on inference and caching servers. Aging it in time gives 2-4x capacity on those classes.

title: Magnonic interference hashes KV keys to merge near-duplicate tokens
idea: Key vectors are injected as microwave phases into a YIG spin-wave interferometer whose fixed geometry implements a random projection. Output-port intensities give locality-sensitive hash bits in nanoseconds. Tokens that land in the same bucket are merged into one averaged KV entry with a count, so redundant context collapses.
why: Long contexts are highly redundant: merging cuts KV memory 2-5x, and spin-wave hashing costs only aJ-scale energy (fact 5).

title: DIMM leasing: pull idle DRAM out of enterprise servers
idea: Inverts 'installed DRAM stays where it was first installed': a telemetry agent shows that enterprise servers use only ~40% of their installed memory. A broker buys or leases the surplus DIMMs, pulls them during maintenance windows and redeploys them to clouds and AI builders.
why: Hundreds of PB of DRAM sit underused in enterprise datacenters; recirculating 10-20% of it equals months of global output.

title: Silicon-carbide NEMS relays form leak-free CAM for KV prefix matching
idea: Build a content-addressable memory from SiC nano-electromechanical relays (contacts demonstrated at 500 C) that stores prompt-prefix hashes. Each request's prefix hash is matched in one cycle, so shared system-prompt KV is reused instead of recomputed and duplicated. The relays have zero off-state leakage, whereas a CMOS CAM leaks heavily at 125 C.
why: Prefix KV dedup cuts KV memory 2-10x for multi-user assistants on hot roadside or cell-tower edge servers.

title: Procure DRAM in touched-byte-hours, not installed gigabytes
idea: Hyperscalers and OEMs size memory contracts and server SKUs from fleet telemetry of touched GB-hours, meaning pages accessed in each 2-minute window. They buy installed DRAM at the 95th percentile of the touched set plus a compressed far tier. Part of what vendors are paid covers effective capacity delivered through compression.
why: Telemetry shows 30-50% of installed DRAM untouched for minutes at a time. Buying to the touched footprint cuts new DIMM purchases 20-35% during the shortage.

title: T-RAM, fixed: replica-tracked thyristor bias for on-die KV window
idea: T-RAM Semiconductor died because thyristor holding current shifts strongly with temperature, ruining margins. Add a per-bank replica thyristor and closed-loop bias generator that tracks temperature and process in real time, and use the dense capacitorless array as an on-die 'hot KV window' for the most recent few thousand tokens.
why: Thyristor cells ~2x denser than SRAM on logic keep hot KV on-die, so less HBM/DRAM is required.

title: Eliminate storage for all-zero cache lines in the memory controller
idea: A per-page 64-bit presence bitmap in the controller marks zero 64B lines, which occupy no DRAM; nonzero lines are packed contiguously and the bitmap is cached on-chip, so a zero-line read costs no DRAM access at all.
why: Post-ReLU activations, sparse tensors and freshly allocated heaps are 30-60% zero lines: 1.3-2x effective capacity and fewer activations per useful bit.

title: Swap fixed GC heap sizing for cluster memory-price-driven heaps
idea: Substitute DRAM headroom with CPU cycles when DRAM is dear. The scheduler publishes a live per-GB memory price, and the JVM, Go, .NET and V8 runtimes read it to retune their heap targets: they collect more often and return pages when memory is expensive and grow when it is cheap. Unchanged hardware.
why: Managed runtimes keep 1.5-3x the live set as headroom. Price-driven sizing reclaims 20-40% of managed-heap DRAM fleet-wide for a few percent of CPU.

title: Demoscene procedural page faults: regenerate data from seeds
idea: From 64 KB demoscene intros that synthesize whole worlds from code: the runtime tags buffers whose content is a deterministic function (RNG-initialized tensors, positional tables, lookup tables, dropout masks, synthetic test data) and stores only a seed plus generator ID. A page-table miss raises a 'procedural fault' that a small generator engine on the memory controller fills on the fly.
why: Trades abundant FLOPs for scarce bytes; removes 10-30% of footprint in training and simulation jobs whose bulk state is regenerable, and eliminates the write traffic for it.

title: Halftone screen: error-diffused 1-bit weights that shrug off flips
idea: Halftone printing renders gray with binary dots plus error diffusion. Weights are binarized with Floyd-Steinberg-style error diffusion along the input dimension, carrying each residual to neighboring weights, and per-block FP16 scales are kept in protected memory. Each output sums thousands of +/-1 weights, so 1% flips act as small additive noise, like a few misprinted dots.
why: At 1 bit per weight (16x smaller than FP16), stored in unprotected 1%-BER cells, the high-grade memory needed for weights falls more than 16x.

title: Zuse Z1 mechanical memory reborn as buckled-beam NEMS bits
idea: Revive the Z1's sliding-plate mechanical memory as university-etched buckled Si or SiN nanobeams with two stable positions: reads sense capacitance to a fixed electrode without moving the beam, and electrostatic pulses snap it over on rare writes.
why: Zero leakage, no refresh (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power) and unlimited reads make a store for weights and static tables that sits outside DRAM.

title: Reflash SSDs to zoned mode, lend freed FTL DRAM via CMB
idea: Box: repurpose × installed NVMe SSDs × controller DRAM (~1 GB per TB) × firmware reflash × NVMe Controller Memory Buffer. Switching drives to zoned/host-managed mapping frees the controller DRAM that held the FTL table, which firmware then exposes to the host as a PCIe-mapped CMB for I/O buffers, queues and spill of warm data.
why: Every installed 30 TB SSD carries ~30 GB of DRAM; reclaiming it adds host-usable memory with zero new wafers, so no new fluorinated etch gases, PFAS resists or fluoropolymer parts are consumed.

title: approx-tagged allocations silently stored at reduced precision
idea: Imposed limit: a bit earns DRAM only if it changes an output. Programmers or compilers tag allocations approx(bits=8); the memory controller transparently stores fp32 data as 8-bit block floating point with shared exponents and expands it on read, so caches and code still see fp32.
why: Graphics, ML activations, sensor data and scientific intermediates tolerate truncation; tagged regions shrink 2-4x with no code rewrite.

title: Eliminate recommender embedding tables with hash-driven embedding generators
idea: Replace TB-scale ID-to-vector tables with deep hash embedding: each ID is hashed by k functions into a dense code, and a small MLP generates its embedding on the fly.
why: Recommendation models are the largest DRAM consumers in many datacenters; tables shrink 100-1000x into GB-scale networks.

title: Precision-resistor mask enabling charge-domain MAC inside commodity DDR
idea: One added thin-film resistor mask gives commodity DDR dies a calibrated charge-sharing reference, enabling bit-serial analog multiply-accumulate on the bitlines. Bandwidth-hungry decode GEMV runs inside the DDR, so weights can live in cheap DDR instead of HBM. Compute moves from the package scale to the bitline scale.
why: HBM costs about 3x the wafer area per bit (fact 6). Moving GEMV into DDR cuts HBM bits needed 2-4x and total memory wafer area per model by about 40%.

title: Bit-plane split: MSBs in silicon, LSBs on glass
idea: The bits of a weight or activation differ in importance by powers of two, so they need not share a medium. Keep sign, exponent and top mantissa bits in silicon DRAM and the low mantissa planes in a glass-TFT tier with relaxed retention and no ECC; both are read in parallel and recombined on the fly, and LSB errors cost little accuracy.
why: Silicon DRAM per tensor drops 40-60% at negligible accuracy loss, with cheap approximate glass bits holding the low-value half.

title: Movable-type rack: lines typeset from a shared CXL slug case
idea: A print shop keeps one case of type and sets any page from it. Here a rack-level CXL memory appliance keeps one copy of each unique 64B line (a 'slug'), indexed by a 64-bit content hash. Each server's page table points to page 'formes', which are lists of slug IDs that the memory controller assembles at read time, with copy-on-write on stores. Read-mostly content (OS images, libraries, model weights, container layers) is then set once per rack instead of once per server.
why: Cuts capacity demand: rack-wide dedup at line rather than page granularity catches the near-identical pages that KSM misses, saving 1.3-3x footprint in VM, container and inference fleets that hold the same bytes in dozens of servers.

title: ER triage nurse: three-tier KV precision with a sink summary token
idea: Triage sorts patients by urgency. Every 256 tokens, accumulated attention mass ranks the cached tokens. Critical tokens stay FP8, stable ones are requantized to 2-bit, and the rest are evicted after their values are folded into a running weighted 'sink' token per head, so their aggregate influence survives.
why: KV memory drops 4-8x at long context with less quality loss than pure eviction, which means more concurrent users per GPU.

title: Core-rope legacy: mask-ROM weight planes for frozen inference models
idea: From the Apollo Guidance Computer's woven core-rope ROM: store a frozen LLM's weights in via-programmed mask-ROM dies (one via present or absent per bit, no capacitor, no refresh) stacked beside the accelerator, so HBM/DRAM holds only activations and KV. A model update re-spins only one or two via/metal masks on a mature node.
why: Weights are often 50-80% of inference memory; a ROM bit needs no capacitor (fact 1) and no refresh (fact 3) and can be ~3-5x cheaper per bit on a mature node, cutting DRAM per served model 2-5x.

title: Eliminate host DRAM staging: GPU servers spec'd with quarter memory
idea: Use GPUDirect Storage loaders so weights and datasets go NVMe-to-HBM directly, and publish an open reference server spec with 256 GB host DRAM instead of 1-2 TB; it is a software plus integration business.
why: Host DRAM in AI servers, much of it staging buffers, is a large and growing DRAM sink; cuts of 4-8x per server are possible.

title: Store context as entropy-coded tokens, regenerate KV on demand
idea: Combine the model's own next-token probabilities with arithmetic coding: cold context is evicted from the KV cache and kept only as token IDs coded at ~1-2 bits per token, and when attention needs a span a burst prefill kernel recomputes its K/V. A tiny per-span key summary decides when recompute is worth it.
why: A token's KV is ~50-300 KB in large models versus under one byte as coded text, so long-context DRAM drops by orders of magnitude, paid for with abundant compute.

title: Printed RFID logbooks unlock a second life for retired DIMMs
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a printed RFID tag with a printed temperature-integrating sensor goes on every DIMM and logs hours, thermal history and correctable-error counts. When servers retire, modules are graded instantly without bench testing and redeployed into lower-tier pools or memory-expansion boxes instead of being shredded.
why: Hyperscalers retire servers after 4-6 years with working DRAM; trustworthy grading could return several percent of annual bit demand to service from existing modules.

title: Eliminate per-layer KV caches by sharing one KV across layer groups
idea: Train models where groups of 2-4 adjacent layers query one shared K/V projection stored once, with small per-layer query adapters for quality.
why: KV memory drops 2-4x architecturally, stacking with quantization and paging.

title: Learned noise-floor zones that truncate float mantissas
idea: Worsen: store every float mantissa bit even below the data's noise floor. Flip: a per-allocation precision tag, set by profiling how many mantissa bits change the output, lets the controller store only the top k bits of each float in packed form and zero-fill on read.
why: Capacity: 1.5-3x for simulation fields, gradients and sensor data where low-order bits are noise.

title: Piezo-steered fiber switches re-home memory blades by demand
idea: Static wiring between memory and servers forces each server to carry its own peak. Fiber cross-connects steered by piezoceramic actuators (no silicon MEMS) rewire whole memory blades between servers every few seconds to minutes, following the scheduler's demand forecast, with the optical path carrying CXL over fiber.
why: Capacity follows demand at rack-to-row scale, so provisioned DRAM per server drops 20-35%, and an attached blade still delivers local latency and full bandwidth.

title: Wide-slow capacity DRAM bins from trailing DRAM lines
idea: Inverts 'DRAM must hit speed bins': existing 2x/1x-nm DDR4 lines run to relaxed timing specs (longer tRCD, lower clock) and allow more repaired rows, tuned for CXL capacity tiers whose latency is already ~200 ns. Looser bins raise yield and the share of each wafer that can be sold.
why: Raises usable bit output of existing trailing DRAM fabs 10-20% and supplies far-memory tiers without leading-edge wafers.

title: Approximate-grade DRAM bins sold for error-tolerant tensors
idea: Dies that fail retention binning or exceed their redundancy still hold 99.999% good bits. Bin and sell them as approximate-grade modules with a published bad-cell map; the OS maps only error-tolerant pages there (NN activations, media, sketches), and the map steers sign and exponent bits onto known-good columns.
why: Raises usable supply by recovering 5-15% of dies that are now scrapped or down-binned, with no new fab capital.

title: Nanoimprint mask-ROM tier for immutable weights and code
idea: Worsen: store frozen model weights and libraries in rewritable, refreshed DRAM. Flip: burn frozen artifacts into ultra-dense 3D mask ROM patterned by nanoimprint (no EUV, no capacitor, no refresh) on swappable cartridges, keeping DRAM for mutable state only.
why: Cost: ROM bits at NAND-like or lower cost give 100x cheaper per GB for read-only data; trades immutability (a new cartridge per model version).

title: Printing-press plates: one copy of model weights serves many hosts
idea: Borrowed from printing, where one plate prints a whole run: a CXL 3.x multi-host shared-memory appliance holds a single read-only copy of popular model weights mapped into 8-32 servers, each of which keeps only KV and activations locally; a hot-row SRAM cache in the switch absorbs repeated reads.
why: Every inference host now stores its own copy of the same 100-800 GB of weights; sharing cuts weight DRAM 8-32x across a pod.

title: Magnifying glass: foveated KV precision around attention focus
idea: Like foveated rendering, the KV manager keeps recent tokens and retrieval anchors at FP8, mid-distance tokens at 3-bit and far tokens merged into learned gist tokens, re-sharpening a region from a flash copy when attention mass returns to it.
why: 4-10x KV footprint reduction on long contexts with bounded quality loss.

title: Certify crypto-erase so retired DIMMs are resold, not shredded
idea: Reverse the security default: a NIST/ISO-certified power-off and pattern-overwrite attestation for volatile DRAM, with signed logs from the server BMC, replaces mandatory physical shredding of memory modules in government and enterprise disposal rules.
why: DRAM is volatile, yet shredding destroys working capacity that could supply the secondary market; every reused GB replaces new fab output that would need neon litho and helium-cooled tools.

title: Rotational molding: scramble stashed activations so flips average to zero
idea: Rotomolding spins the mold on two axes so material deposits evenly, with no bias. DRAM retention failures are one-directional (charged cells lose charge), which biases the value errors. Activations saved for backprop are therefore stored at 4 bits in 1%-BER cells, XORed with a PRNG mask whose per-block seed lets the mask be regenerated on read. A charge-loss flip then means +2^k or -2^k with equal probability, so the noise is zero-mean and gradients stay unbiased, only slightly noisier than SGD already is.
why: The activation stash is the largest training memory consumer; an unprotected 4-bit stash cuts it about 4x and moves it to cheap cells without checkpoint recompute.

title: Phosphorus ATP trade: spend FLOPs, store KV for every fourth layer
idea: ATP is the cell's currency for spending energy instead of storing work; the model stores KV only for layers 0, 4, 8 and so on, and a small adapter MLP co-trained with the model predicts the skipped layers' K and V from the nearest stored layer at attention time for ~3% extra FLOPs.
why: KV cache dominates long-context serving memory; a 3.5-4x KV reduction lets each GPU hold 3-4x more context or users (density, cost/bit).

title: Hearing-aid retrofit: compressing buffer chips reflowed onto existing RDIMMs
idea: Retrofit rather than replace: swap the data-buffer/RCD chips on installed DDR5 RDIMMs (rework <260 C) for pin-compatible buffers that compress lines inline and advertise larger capacity through SPD, so existing DIMMs grow ~1.5x without new DRAM dies.
why: Capacity uplift on the installed base using only low-temperature assembly, deployable by US rework shops within months.

title: Genome-like health ledger travels with every memory module
idea: Each module stores a tamper-evident lifetime record (hours, temperature, ECC events, hammer counts, repairs) in extended SPD, like DNA carrying heritable history, readable by any buyer or recycler to price and place the module in its next life; mandated in procurement standards.
why: Secondary-market liquidity: makes used DRAM trustworthy, raising reuse rates and lowering new-bit demand.

title: Tunneling-leak gain cells make old KV tokens fade like ALiBi
idea: Store KV entries in gain cells whose tunneling oxide is deliberately thin, so charge decays with a time constant of a few hundred tokens. Each read value is then naturally scaled by exp(-age/tau), which is exactly a recency-bias attention prior. Cells whose signal drops below the sense threshold are reclaimed as free slots, with no refresh or eviction logic.
why: Gives refresh-free KV memory (fact 3) that reclaims its own capacity. Expect a 3-8x smaller KV footprint for long contexts, where distant tokens are down-weighted anyway.

title: Admit LLM requests by predicted KV-seconds, not arrival order
idea: Reverse the scheduler's input: a small regressor predicts each request's output length and context so the scheduler admits and orders work by predicted KV-byte-seconds (shortest-KV-first, with preemption) instead of FIFO, bounding peak KV rather than provisioning for it.
why: Peak KV memory falls ~1.5-2x at equal throughput, delivered as a software update on installed accelerators.

title: Minify the page: 64-byte cache-line-granular paging
idea: Minify the paging unit from 4 KB to 64 B: the memory controller keeps per-line access bits and a line-level remap table, evicting never-touched lines inside 'hot' pages to a compressed CXL/flash tier while the page stays mapped. A miss to an evicted line is refilled by hardware in ~1 us without an OS fault.
why: Attacks page overfetch at the capacity level: 30-60% of lines in resident 4 KB pages are typically cold, so the DRAM needed shrinks ~1.5-2.5x for the same working set.

title: Hot-line consolidation: memory tiering at 64-byte granularity
idea: Po: the page is one byte. The memory/CXL controller tracks hotness per cache line and migrates hot lines out of mostly-cold pages into dense hot-line pages in DRAM through a line-remap table, leaving cold remainders in compressed or far memory.
why: Page-granular tiering keeps 4 KB resident for a few hot lines; line-level consolidation shrinks the DRAM tier 2-3x for sparse-access workloads (fact 8 overfetch).

title: Minify precision to ternary: 5-trits-per-byte packing in controller
idea: Minify weights to native ternary (1.58-bit) models. The memory controller packs 5 trits per byte (3^5=243) and unpacks into add/subtract-only matmul units, with no multipliers.
why: ~10x fewer weight bits than FP16 and lower data-movement energy, on the same DRAM parts.

title: Position-free KV storage for cross-user chunk dedup
idea: The same RAG documents and system prompts recur across users at different offsets, which defeats prefix caching. Store each chunk's keys before RoPE, under a content hash; apply the rotary rotation for the real position at read time, and run a small learned correction pass over the first few tokens of each chunk to restore cross-chunk attention.
why: In RAG-heavy serving, KV for shared corpora is stored once per cluster instead of once per request: 5-20x less KV capacity.

title: No.1 ESS program-store/call-store split by page write rate
idea: The 1965 No.1 ESS kept programs in a read-mostly twistor 'program store' and live call data in a small writable ferrite 'call store'. Revive the split: the hypervisor classifies pages by measured write rate, placing read-mostly pages (weights, code, static tables) on denser memories with slow or endurance-limited writes (NOR-like, ReRAM, PCM) and only write-hot pages in DRAM.
why: Read-mostly data is 50-70% of AI server bytes; memories that fail as DRAM replacements on endurance become DRAM capacity substitutes, cutting DRAM per server 40-60%.

title: Holographic recall: attention keys searched in NV analog CAM
idea: Like holographic associative memories returning the stored image closest to a probe, store KV keys in a FeFET/ReRAM analog content-addressable array that computes query-key similarity in place and returns top-k token addresses; only those k values are read from NV value storage.
why: Long-context KV becomes non-volatile and sparsely accessed; KV DRAM need drops 10x+ and attention scan energy falls.

title: Pyroelectric film images row heat to steer page tiering
idea: Deposit a thin LiTaO3 pyroelectric layer over each DRAM bank, patterned into per-subarray pixels. Activation bursts heat their rows by millikelvins; each pixel emits charge proportional to dT/dt, and a tiny integrator turns that into a hotness map. The OS keeps only the hottest 20-30% of pages in DRAM and pushes cold pages to compressed CXL or flash, with no SRAM access counters or page-table sampling.
why: Gives tiering hardware-free access tracking. Cuts DRAM per server 30-40% for <1% area and no extra periphery (fact 7).

title: Minify optimizer state from 16 bytes to ~2.5 bytes/param
idea: Minify training memory: FP8 weights with stochastic rounding (no FP32 master copy), 4-bit block-quantized first moments and factored (row/column) second moments, fused into the optimizer kernel.
why: Optimizer and master-weight state dominates training DRAM/HBM. Per-parameter bytes drop ~6x, so the same model trains on far fewer HBM stacks.

title: Eliminate full-precision KV for stale tokens with age-tiered quantization
idea: An inference kernel library re-quantizes KV in the background as tokens age: the newest 512 tokens stay at fp16, older ones drop to int4, and the oldest to 2-bit with per-channel outlier rescue.
why: Long-context KV memory falls 4-6x with a small quality loss concentrated on distant tokens.

title: Printed coded-aperture masks capture images pre-compressed
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a roll-to-roll printed pseudo-random amplitude mask in front of the sensor performs compressive sensing optically, so the sensor reads 10-25% as many measurements as pixels and the buffer stores only those measurements. Full frames are reconstructed only when a downstream detector flags one.
why: Camera fleets and robots buffer raw frames in DRAM; compressing optically at capture cuts frame-buffer DRAM 4-10x.

title: Construction foreman's just-in-time delivery: router-lookahead MoE expert paging
idea: Foremen have steel delivered the day it is bolted up. A small predictor reads layer L's hidden state and forecasts which experts layers L+1 to L+3 will route to. Those experts are DMA'd from host RAM or NVMe via GPUDirect Storage just in time, and HBM keeps only a hot-expert cache. Software-only, open-source.
why: MoE models keep every expert resident while each token uses ~5% of them. Lookahead paging cuts weight HBM 3-6x for open MoE models on commodity GPUs.

title: Near-duplicate pages stored as deltas to a canonical library
idea: Worsen: store thousands of pages that differ in only a few bytes as full copies. Flip: the controller fingerprints pages with similarity hashes, keeps a library of canonical base pages, and stores each similar page as a compressed XOR delta against its base.
why: Capacity: 2-4x for VM fleets, object headers and serialized records where exact dedup misses near-identical data.

title: HBM stealing: idle neighbor GPUs host overflow KV blocks
idea: Reverse the swap direction from down-to-host to sideways-to-peers: a cluster daemon tracks free HBM on each GPU and pages KV blocks into idle neighbors over NVLink/ICI, ~10x faster than host DDR, before any new memory is bought.
why: GPU fleets often leave 20-40% of HBM unused on some devices; pooling it raises usable capacity by that margin in software alone, with no gas-consuming fabrication.

title: Output-entropy-gated KV precision on existing hardware
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: the serving loop watches each request's next-token entropy; while the model is confident, new KV is stored at INT2-INT3, and when entropy spikes it switches to INT8 and re-quantizes recent blocks, a closed loop that spends bits only where uncertainty demands. It runs as software on hardware already deployed.
why: Average KV width drops from 16 bits to ~3 bits with a quality guard; ~4-5x KV capacity, no new silicon.

title: Exascale memory futures market inside the cluster scheduler
idea: From exascale centers where bytes-per-flop keep falling: jobs bid for GB-hours in a real-time internal market with futures contracts, jobs that release memory early earn credits, and the scheduler auctions stranded DRAM to preemptible opportunistic jobs.
why: Fleets strand 20-40% of DRAM through static reservations; pricing exposes it so operators can buy 20-30% fewer DIMMs.

title: Goto-pair tunnel-diode CAM as hardware hash-cons index
idea: Revive the 1960s Goto pair, two series tunnel diodes that latch a bit with no transistor, as the storage element of a CAM cell: Esaki diodes made by degenerate spin-on doping in a university fab form a dense CAM that holds content hashes and answers 'is this block already stored?' in one cycle for inline memory dedup.
why: Inline dedup needs a huge, fast hash index that today eats DRAM; a native associative store makes dedup feasible at memory speed, 1.3-3x effective capacity on duplicate-heavy servers.

title: Pruned-to-customer MoE: deploy only the experts real traffic wakes
idea: Po: a customer only needs the experts they actually use. Each domestic deployment profiles a week of its own traffic, drops experts with negligible routing mass, patches the router with a small distilled fix-up for residual tokens, and serves the slimmed MoE on U.S.-made hardware.
why: Domain traffic typically activates a minority of experts; pruning 50-70% of them shrinks weight memory in proportion with small task-quality loss.

title: Model-emitted page-out tokens let the model page its KV
idea: Reverse who manages the cache: fine-tune the model to emit special <page-out span> and <page-in topic> tokens, so it moves the KV of finished sub-tasks to host storage and recalls it itself, like a program managing its own overlays.
why: Long agentic sessions keep only their working set resident: 3-10x less KV in HBM with software on existing hardware, so no new neon- or helium-dependent fab output is needed.

title: Swap small tokenizers for vocabulary transplants that shrink KV per text
idea: Substitute a 32k-token vocabulary with a 200k+ one tuned to code and multilingual text: new embeddings are initialized from compositions of old-token embeddings, then a short fine-tune follows. The same document becomes fewer tokens, so fewer KV entries.
why: KV memory scales with token count; 25-40% fewer tokens for code and non-English text cuts the KV cache proportionally on every request.

title: Single coherent copy shared by CPU, GPU and NIC kills bounce buffers
idea: Box: eliminate copies × coherent fabric × buffer × allocation time × one physical copy over CXL.cache or chip-to-chip links. Pipelines that hold the same tensor in pinned host memory, GPU memory and NIC staging use one coherent allocation with zero-copy DMA.
why: Staging and bounce buffers occupy 10–30% of host DRAM in AI servers; removing two of three copies frees most of it.

title: Swap raw bf16 in HBM for ANS-coded tensors decoded at load
idea: Substitute raw storage with entropy-coded storage. An asymmetric-numeral-system decoder in the GPU's L2-to-SM path, driven by a per-tile offset table, lets weights and KV live entropy-coded in HBM and expand transparently on load. bf16 exponents carry only ~2.6 bits of entropy, and activation tiles are often sparse.
why: A lossless 1.3-1.6x capacity gain on weights, more on sparse tensors, plus fewer pJ per useful bit moved (fact 5).

title: Micron Automata Processor reborn as CXL-side predicate filter
idea: Micron's in-DRAM NFA Automata Processor died as a standalone PCIe card with proprietary tooling and no killer app. Embed the NFA/predicate fabric inside a CXL memory expander and compile it from standard SQL WHERE clauses and regexes (DuckDB/Postgres plugin), so scans run where cold tables live and only matching rows enter host DRAM.
why: Host DRAM working set for analytics shrinks by the filter selectivity (often 10-100x); cold tables stay on cheaper far memory.

title: Weights as wires: models compiled into fixed logic on 18A
idea: Po: the weights are welded into the chip. A frozen model is synthesized into constant-coefficient multiplier/adder trees (weights folded into gates, shared partial products via canonical-signed-digit recoding) on Intel 18A or Samsung Taylor (TX) 2 nm and packaged in the U.S.; only KV and activations need DRAM.
why: Removes weight storage and weight fetch entirely: DRAM per inference node drops by the weight share (50-90%) and energy per token ~10x, using U.S. logic fabs instead of foreign DRAM.

title: ZFS dedup's RAM hunger, fixed: flash-resident delta store for fine-tunes
idea: ZFS dedup became notorious for needing ~5 GB of RAM per TB for its dedup table. Serve thousands of fine-tuned model variants by content-defined chunking of weight tensors into flash, with an SRAM cuckoo filter (~1 byte per chunk) to spot duplicate chunks and a flash-resident index, so each variant costs only its unique delta.
why: Multi-tenant fine-tune serving without N copies in DRAM: 10-100x fewer bytes for near-identical variants.

title: Bear hibernation: migrate idle rows to NVM before retention expires
idea: Borrowed from hibernating animals that drop to near-zero metabolism: the controller timestamps each row's last activation and, when an untouched row nears its retention deadline, moves it once into a dense non-volatile tier and marks it hibernating instead of refreshing it; a later access wakes it back into DRAM.
why: Periodic refresh becomes a one-time migration of cold rows; DRAM holds only the awake working set (often 20-40% of allocated), shrinking provisioned DRAM with zero refresh power.

title: Minify indexes 100x with piecewise-linear learned indexes
idea: Minify B-tree internal nodes and hash directories into PGM-style piecewise-linear models with guaranteed error windows. Each lookup does one model step and one bounded scan.
why: Index memory falls 10-1000x, and databases where indexes dominate the DRAM footprint gain >=10x.

title: Rack-wide deduplicated page cache in one pooled memory box
idea: Move the OS file page cache, which often fills 30-50% of server DRAM with the same container layers, binaries and datasets, out of every host into one rack-level CXL memory pool indexed by file-content hash; hosts map those pages read-only.
why: One copy per rack instead of one per host: 20-40% less DRAM per server in container-heavy fleets.

title: Andon cord: fast raw reads, full decode only when confidence drops
idea: Toyota workers pull the andon cord to stop the line only when they see a defect. Weights sit in 1%-BER memory under a systematic LDPC whose data bits are usable as-is, so the fast path reads only the data bits and skips parity. When the model's token entropy or logit margin crosses an anomaly threshold, the step is re-run on parity-decoded weights.
why: Gives cheap-cell capacity with no decode latency on more than 99% of steps, and limits quality loss to rare anomalous steps, at about 12% parity instead of duplicate copies.

title: Octopus-arm memory modules reduce data before it reaches the host
idea: Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons live in its arms; likewise CXL memory expanders carry local filter, aggregate, top-k and embedding-pooling engines so the host receives answers rather than raw rows, eliminating host-side staging buffers and duplicate working copies.
why: Host DRAM and data movement: 2-4x less host buffer memory for analytics and recommendation, 5-10x less link traffic.

title: Silver-halide latents: training activations saved as compact neural latents
idea: Film stores a faint silver latent image that development amplifies; during training each checkpointed activation tile is encoded by a small learned encoder into a 16x smaller latent written to DRAM and decoded on chip in the backward pass, with the codec co-trained to keep gradient error bounded.
why: Activations dominate training memory; 16x smaller latents cut activation DRAM ~10x and DRAM bits written and read per activation >10x, with the codec costing far less energy than the traffic it removes (energy, density).

title: Deterministic lockstep replay replaces resident state for idle actors
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: store idle entities (game objects, agents, session actors, simulation cells) in the time dimension, keeping only their input event log since the last checkpoint, and regenerate state by deterministic replay when touched, the way 1997-era RTS games synchronized by inputs only.
why: Idle actor state is often 60-90% of resident memory in stateful backends and logs are 10-100x smaller than state; needs no new hardware.

title: Zero-word bitmaps so DRAM never stores a zero
idea: Worsen: burn full DRAM cells on the zeros that fill 20-40% of real heaps. Flip: the memory controller keeps a per-line 8-bit zero-word bitmap in a small tag store and packs only the non-zero words into variable-size slots, so an all-zero line costs no DRAM at all and a mostly-zero line costs a fraction.
why: Capacity: 15-35% fewer GB on sparse heaps, tensors and freshly allocated pages, with no software change; also less refresh and fewer activations.

title: Eliminate Python object boxing with tagged-pointer CPython build
idea: A drop-in CPython fork encodes small ints and floats as tagged pointers and stores homogeneous lists as unboxed typed arrays, keeping C-API compatibility through lazy boxing.
why: Numeric-heavy Python data pipelines use 2-4x less memory, recovering a large hidden DRAM consumer in ML preprocessing.

title: Gold standard: spot-priced GB-seconds that make apps shed memory
idea: Clouds price memory per GB-second at a spot rate tied to fleet DRAM utilization, unbundled from vCPU, and expose an API so applications bid for cache size; elastic caches (Redis, JVM heaps, KV caches) shrink automatically when the price rises, and providers sell memory futures to large tenants.
why: Bundled VM pricing hides memory cost, so 30-50% of provisioned DRAM sits idle; real prices plus elastic APIs could free ~20-30% of fleet DRAM with no hardware (capital, cost/bit).

title: Plasmid-style updatable row-hammer defenses extend old dense DRAM
idea: Bacteria swap plasmids to gain new resistances; the CXL or buffer controller carries an embedded FPGA region whose hammer-tracking logic is updated over the air as new access patterns emerge, so vulnerable modules are patched rather than replaced.
why: Row hammer (~1k activations): avoids premature retirement of dense modules and keeps the reuse market viable.

title: Swap stored weight matrices for an on-chip PRNG weight synthesizer
idea: Substitute stored bits with regenerated bits. Each weight block is post-fit as a few coefficients times matrices from a seeded LFSR basis, and a hardware synthesizer next to the tensor cores regenerates the block in SRAM from (seed, coefficients) at use time. DRAM holds only seeds and coefficients.
why: Trades cheap logic for scarce DRAM. About 3-4 bits per weight equivalent cuts weight DRAM 4-5x versus bf16 and cuts transfer energy (fact 5).

title: Rack-wide content-addressed page pool for weights and libraries
idea: IFR: each distinct byte exists once per rack. Closest: a CXL memory pool indexes immutable 2 MB pages (model weights, container layers, shared libraries, JIT code) by 128-bit hash; every host maps them read-only through a small local cache, with copy-on-write on modification.
why: Inference racks replicate 70-400 GB of identical weights per server; 8-16 hosts sharing one copy recovers 40-70% of rack weight DRAM.

title: ISA-level compressed references for every language
idea: Worsen: make every pointer 64 bits even when a heap is under 32 GB. Flip: add region-base registers and load/store forms that widen 32-bit compressed references on the fly in the address-generation unit, so C++, Rust, Go and Python runtimes all get Java-style compressed pointers without software decode.
why: Capacity: 20-40% smaller pointer-heavy heaps (graphs, trees, object graphs) and more useful bits per cache line.

title: Biologist's genome thinking: grow embeddings from hashed IDs, not tables
idea: A genome stores the recipe, not the organism. Recommendation and retrieval embedding tables, often terabytes, are replaced by a generator: several universal hashes of an ID feed a small dense MLP that expresses the embedding on demand. An exact side table remains only for the hottest ~0.1% of IDs.
why: Embedding tables are the largest DRAM consumers in ad and recsys fleets. Generator embeddings shrink them 100-1000x for ~1-3% extra FLOPs, moving cost from scarce DRAM to cheap compute.

title: Audio-RAM revival: partially defective DRAM for error-tolerant data
idea: In the 1980s DRAMs with bad bits were sold as 'ARAM' for answering machines. Revive it: dies and HBM stacks that fail test get a stored fault map and are sold for error-tolerant data, with the allocator putting activations, gradients and low-order weight bits on faulty regions and sign/exponent bits on clean ones.
why: Supply: turns part of the 20-30% HBM/DRAM yield loss into usable cheap capacity, adding several percent to world bit supply with no new fab.

title: Airline overbooking for RAM: overcommit by measured no-show rate
idea: Hypervisors record, per application class, the fraction of allocated memory never touched ('no-shows') and overbook physical DRAM by that rate, with a pre-agreed bump protocol (compress, then demote to CXL flash) for rare oversubscription and a yield-managed premium for guaranteed seats.
why: Cloud VMs often touch only 40-60% of allocated RAM; statistical overbooking could cut provisioned DRAM per VM 25-40%.

title: Offset-trim implant enabling 2-bit cells only for millisecond-lived data
idea: One added halo/Vt implant mask tightens sense-amp transistor mismatch enough for 4-level sensing. Cells store 2 bits only for data that lives shorter than the shortened MLC retention of ~4-8 ms: in-flight activations and current-step scratch. Before that deadline, the allocator demotes any surviving data to 1-bit mode. Data lifetime is matched to cell retention.
why: Ephemeral data is 20-40% of accelerator working memory. Doubling its bits per cell gives 1.2-1.4x capacity per die.

title: Tidal memory: scheduler pairs anti-correlated job footprints
idea: Combine the cluster scheduler with per-job memory-phase profiles: co-locate jobs whose peak footprints alternate in time (nightly ETL vs daytime serving, train vs eval phases) and shuttle the idle job's pages to a CXL/compressed tier at each phase boundary.
why: Servers are provisioned for each job's peak; sharing peaks across time cuts installed DRAM 25-40% fleet-wide.

title: Club sandwich: hybrid-bonded SRAM decks swallow activations
idea: Stack more layers in the sandwich: hybrid-bond (<300 C) 2-4 dense SRAM dies onto the accelerator, sized to keep a full transformer block's activations and the hottest KV pages on-package so they never spill to HBM.
why: Cuts HBM capacity needed per accelerator 20-40% and avoids TSV-heavy HBM stacks (fact 6) for working buffers.

title: Erasure coding replaces triple replication in in-memory stores
idea: Combine storage-style Reed-Solomon coding with in-memory data grids (Redis, parameter servers, session stores): keep k data shards plus m parity shards across nodes and update parity with RDMA-shipped XOR deltas on writes instead of holding three full DRAM replicas.
why: Replica memory falls from 3x to ~1.5x for the same failure tolerance.

title: Birth-tiering allocator places objects by predicted lifetime and heat
idea: IFR: DRAM holds only bytes about to be touched. Closest: allocation call-site, type and stack-hash features feed a tiny on-CPU model that predicts each object's heat; predicted-cold objects are born directly in CXL or flash-backed memory and never migrate, so hot and cold objects never share a page.
why: Page-granular tiering strands 30-50% of near DRAM on mixed hot/cold pages; object-level birth placement cuts near DRAM 30-40%.

title: Mask-ROM foundation models: freeze the weights in vias
idea: Po: RAM is read-only. Frozen, widely deployed model weights are fabricated as via-programmed multi-level mask ROM (only one or two masks change per model) on cheap mature-node wafers stacked under the accelerator; DRAM holds only activations and KV.
why: Weights are 50-90% of inference memory; ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and ~1-2 custom masks, cutting weight cost/bit several-fold and freeing DRAM for KV.

title: Execute-in-place code tier: domestic NOR serves read-only program text
idea: Po: there is no NAND fab in America, so use the flash America still makes. Infineon Austin (TX) NOR flash on a CXL card is mapped as byte-addressable read-only memory, and the loader maps code segments, shared libraries and read-only data directly from it (execute-in-place) so they never occupy DRAM.
why: Code and read-only data are 10-25% of microservice footprints; XIP from domestic NOR (100 ns-class reads, CPU-cached) frees that DRAM with no NAND imports.

title: IGZO panel sums embedding rows in place by current mode
idea: Recommender inference gathers dozens of embedding rows only to sum them, so only the sum matters. Store the embedding tables in IGZO 2T gain cells on display glass and activate every row of a lookup batch at once, so read currents add on shared column lines and a column ADC returns the pooled vector directly.
why: TB-scale embedding tables move from silicon DRAM onto glass, and only one vector per lookup crosses the link (20-80x less traffic).

title: Fuzzy cross-request KV merging with sparse residual patches
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: beyond exact prefix sharing, the serving engine clusters KV blocks from concurrent requests whose vectors differ by less than epsilon (same retrieved chunks at different offsets after RoPE de-rotation, templated prompts) and stores one canonical block plus a sparse INT4 residual per request. A radix tree keyed on locality-sensitive hashes finds merge candidates.
why: RAG and agent workloads re-ingest the same chunks at varying positions where exact prefix caching misses; 2-5x KV memory reduction in multi-tenant serving.

title: Briggs log-table interpolation for cross-layer KV cache
idea: Henry Briggs printed logarithms only at anchor points plus difference columns for interpolation. Store full KV only for anchor layers (every 4th) and, for in-between layers, a per-head low-rank correction to the linear interpolation of the neighbouring anchors' KV, reconstructed on the fly in the read path.
why: KV capacity 2.5-3.5x smaller with the correction term holding accuracy, and stackable with quantization.

title: Sleep consolidation: idle-time compression of agent memory into gist tokens
idea: Borrowed from hippocampal sleep replay and spaced repetition: when an agent session idles, a background pass replays older context through the model to distill each chunk into a few learned gist tokens, keeping full-fidelity KV only for items retrieved repeatedly (high recall strength) and dropping the rest.
why: Long-lived agent contexts are mostly parked KV; consolidation claims 10-50x less resident KV for idle sessions.

title: Acoustic delay-line FIFOs buffer pipeline-parallel activations
idea: Pipeline-stage activations and switch packet buffers are strictly first-in-first-out, so they do not need random-access cells. Store them as surface acoustic waves on lithium-niobate or quartz: at ~3.5 km/s a 2 cm line holds ~6 us, and 1,000 parallel 5 GHz channels in recirculating, re-amplified loops hold ~30 Mbit.
why: Frees MB-scale HBM and DRAM buffers in deep-buffer switches and pipeline stages. The capacity is small, but every byte moved out of HBM also avoids its ~3x wafer tax.

title: Leak-toward-zero encoding turns thermal retention loss into harmless pruning
idea: DRAM charge leaks only one way (true cells go 1 to 0). Store neural weights in sign-magnitude with magnitude bits in true cells and the sign bit in robust NVM, so any leakage flip at 125 C can only shrink a weight's magnitude, which acts like gentle pruning. Error-tolerant tensors then live in banks with 4-8x relaxed refresh.
why: Recovers refresh bandwidth and energy (fact 3) and removes the guard-band overprovisioning hot designs carry. Expect ~20-30% less DRAM for the same delivered bandwidth.

title: Sushi conveyor: CNT logic over DRAM decodes compressed KV in place
idea: Dishes pass the chef on a belt: deposit carbon-nanotube FET logic (<=325 C) on top of the DRAM array's metal stack so 2-bit compressed KV rows passing the sense amps are decoded and dot-producted with the query right there, returning only scores and selected values.
why: KV can live at 2-bit density permanently (4-8x capacity) because decompressed copies never need buffer space; also cuts data movement (fact 5).
